claims.text: The starting WTaVTi precursor is nominally equiatomic.
The precursor is a single-BCC, directionally solidified alloy with W/Ta-rich dendrites and Ti/V-rich interdendritic channels.
Immersion in molten Cu at 1200 °C for 96 h selectively extracts Ti from the WTaVTi precursor.
Liquid-metal dealloying produces a bicontinuous, directionally aligned RHEA–Cu structure.
The resulting composite contains approximately 64 vol.% BCC RHEA ligaments and 36 vol.% near-pure FCC Cu channels.
Approximately 300 nm W-rich interlayers form spontaneously at the RHEA/Cu interfaces.
Minor HCP Ti-rich precipitates are present in the dealloyed composite.
Ti migrates preferentially into molten Cu because Ti and Cu have a negative heat of mixing.
Preferential Ti extraction leaves a refractory network composed primarily of W, Ta, and V.
Continued Ti extraction causes formation of the W-rich passivating interlayer.
Directionally aligned Cu channels establish efficient heat-conduction pathways.
The W-rich interlayer suppresses further interfacial exchange and interfacial void formation.
The W-rich interlayer prevents undesirable phase separation.
The complex RHEA lattice alters defect dynamics in a way that resists helium-induced swelling.
Above approximately 650 °C, the dealloyed composite will have substantially higher thermal conductivity than the untreated WTaVTi precursor.
Above approximately 650 °C, the dealloyed composite will outperform conventional W–Cu composites in thermal conductivity.
The dealloyed composite is expected to exceed the thermal conductivity of pure W beyond 1000 °C.
Under 25 keV He+ irradiation up to approximately 8–8.5 × 10^17 atoms cm−2, the dealloyed composite will show less swelling and blistering than the untreated precursor and pure W.
Thermal-conductivity behavior above 1000 °C is based on extrapolation from measurements extending only to approximately 800 °C.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis says the intervention prevents phase separation, while the proposed product is explicitly a two-phase BCC-RHEA/FCC-Cu structure. This is reconcilable only if 'phase separation' means undesirable macroscopic segregation rather than the intended nanoscale or microscale two-phase architecture, but that distinction is not stated.
